reports.name: Junior Caminero
reports.published_report: Forty-six home runs projected at age 23, on a .918 OPS, and the Statcast contact quality almost undersells the power: a .517 xSLG and 93.0 mph average exit velocity put him in rarefied air for a hitter his age. The walk rate at 12.2% is genuinely good, the strikeout rate at 18.3% is fine, and the chase and whiff numbers sit near league average, which means the bat-to-ball profile isn't a liability dragging against the raw damage. The one real blemish is the fielding, where an OAA percentile of 1 suggests he may eventually get pushed off third base entirely. If the glove forces a position change and the defensive value evaporates, you're still left with an offensive force; if he sticks at third, you're looking at one of the game's most complete young hitters.

reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
reports.published_report: The .365 xwOBA and 49.7% hard-hit rate tell you the bat is genuinely loud, but the 26.6% strikeout rate is the friction in the whole profile. What makes the package work anyway is the 11.7% walk rate holding up alongside that contact volatility, because it keeps the .369 OBP real even in the stretches where he's chasing at a 34.2% clip. Add 29.5 ft/s sprint speed and the projection's 39 stolen bases aren't optimism, they're arithmetic. The question isn't whether he's an impact player, it's whether the chase rate drifts higher and starts cutting into the power-speed combination that makes 34 home runs and 39 steals plausible from the same guy.

reports.name: James Wood
reports.published_report: The xwOBA is .419 and the barrel rate is 20.8%, both sitting at the 99th and 100th percentiles — that's not a profile you describe carefully, it's one you just read straight. Wood hits the ball as hard as anyone in baseball, walks at 16.8% while chasing only 21.7% of pitches outside the zone, and the contact quality is so extreme that a .585 xSLG makes the projection's .523 SLG look conservative. The problem is the 28.6% strikeout rate, which is the only thing standing between this and a canonical offensive profile, and if pitchers find a consistent way to exploit the 30.7% whiff rate once the league adjusts, the walk and power numbers are what remains. At 23, with that exit velocity and plate discipline already in place, the projection of 37 home runs and a .387 OBP in 684 plate appearances is the floor scenario if the swing-and-miss stays stubborn, and the ceiling is somewhere most 23-year-olds don't get to visit.

reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: The xwOBA tells you everything you need to know about both sides: .413 as a hitter, .257 as a pitcher, each sitting at the 94th percentile or better. At the plate, a 16.8% barrel rate and 13.9% walk rate produce contact quality that almost nobody touches, and the 22.8% strikeout rate is a real cost but one the .395 OBP absorbs without complaint. On the mound, a 2.71 xERA and 30.4% whiff rate against a 7.6% walk rate sketch a legitimate top-of-the-rotation arm, the whole profile hinging on staying healthy enough to accumulate starts after the Tommy John recovery. The projection, .291/.395/.557 with 39 home runs across 689 plate appearances, only looks aggressive until you run his Statcast card; then it looks like what happens when elite contact quality meets full-time at-bats in a Dodgers lineup.

reports.name: Elly De La Cruz
reports.published_report: The contact-quality profile here is genuinely elite, and the strikeout rate is the one thing standing between him and a perennial All-Star conversation. A 94.0 mph average exit velocity sits at the 98th percentile, and a 14.7% barrel rate backs it up — this isn't a guy running empty hard contact. The .368 xwOBA says the underlying production matches the exit velocity shape even as a 26.9% strikeout rate keeps the surface numbers from reflecting it in full. If the chase rate (25.7%) continues to improve and the strikeouts drift down, the projection's .843 OPS with 27 home runs and 33 stolen stolen bases becomes a floor rather than a ceiling; if the swing-and-miss holds at this level, he's a volatile high-upside piece who costs you a batting average in the spots he goes quiet.

reports.name: Kade Anderson
reports.published_report: A 1.20 ERA and 0.70 WHIP across 82.3 innings at AA is the kind of line that makes you check whether the level is right, and the translation says it is. Anderson's 12 walks against 119 strikeouts produce a K-BB% that translates to 21.4% in a league where the average starter sits at 13.5%, and his translated walk rate of 2.1 per nine lands more than a full walk below the MLB mean. The command is the spine of the profile: if it plays up in the majors the way it's played at AA, you're looking at a mid-rotation arm or better; if the stuff gets exposed against better hitters and the walks climb toward league average, you're left with a multi-inning arm who misses enough bats to stick. One to two years out, with this much control at this age, the floor alone is worth something.

reports.name: Daylen Lile
reports.published_report:
The sprint speed is elite. Everything else is the problem.

reports.name: Brayan Rocchio
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile is almost entirely below average, and the one thing keeping this from being a pure out-generator is contact. A 14.5% strikeout rate is genuinely elite, and Rocchio makes consistent enough contact to push his xBA to .243 even with 86.5 mph average exit velocity and a 3.0% barrel rate that sits near the bottom of the league. The projection accounts for all of this: .255/.322/.381 across 613 projected PA is a second-division regular line, sustained almost entirely by the bat-to-ball skill, league-average speed, and what the 99th-percentile OAA says is exceptional glove work at shortstop. If the contact rate erodes or the chase rate climbs past its current 33.0%, the offensive floor drops fast and the glove becomes the whole argument for roster standing.

reports.name: Carter Jensen
reports.published_report: The contact profile is genuinely broken: a .203 xBA and a 30.1% whiff rate that sits in the bottom fifth of the league. The bat-to-ball problem isn't subtle. What saves the argument is that when Jensen does connect, the ball moves — 90.6 mph average exit velocity and a 10.1% barrel rate suggest real pop, and that translates to a projected 21 home runs and a .414 SLG across 596 plate appearances. He also walks at a 9.6% clip and chases just 26.0% of pitches outside the zone, so the plate discipline isn't the issue. The profile hinges on whether he can cut the whiff rate enough to let the underlying contact quality surface; if he can't, a .230/.304/.414 line at catcher is a serviceable regular, but one strikeout spike away from a lineup problem.

reports.name: Lazaro Montes
reports.published_report: Thirty-two home runs across AAA & AA at 21, with a .314 ISO that translates to .213 against MLB pitching — that's the loud part of this profile, and it's believable across 450 plate appearances. The problem is the strikeout rate: 31% in the minors translates directly to 31% against MLB arms, landing in the 16th percentile of the hitter pool, and a contact floor that makes the .367 OBP fragile the moment the walks dry up. Montes has 65 walks in that sample, so the discipline shows up, and the .561 slugging earns its place, but this entire profile hinges on whether the power is loud enough to carry a strikeout rate that will get exposed against quality spin. reports.name: Andrés Muñoz
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate sits at 36.9% and the whiff rate is at the very top of the sport, and those two numbers are essentially the whole argument for Andrés Muñoz as a legitimate closer. The 99.5 mph fastball is what generates a 37.5% chase rate that ranks among the best in baseball, and when hitters do make contact, the 43.0% hard-hit rate is a real tension point — the stuff misses bats at an elite clip, but the contact allowed carries more juice than you'd want. The walk rate at 9.7% is the lever: if that number creeps up, the hard contact that does land starts to matter a lot more, and a 3.28 xERA becomes something uglier. He's a genuine closer if the command holds, a high-leverage question mark if it doesn't.

reports.name: Jhoan Duran
reports.published_report: The .232 xwOBA and 2.21 xERA sit at the 99th percentile, and the walk rate of 3.8% is literally perfect by Statcast's scale — there is almost no profile cleaner than this one. Duran's 36.5% strikeout rate and 37.0% whiff rate coexist with a barrel rate of just 3.4%, which explains how a 42.2% hard-hit rate ends up doing so little damage: hitters are making loud contact on pitches they've already been fooled by, off-balance and late. The projection calls for 34 saves with a 2.07 ERA over 59.1 innings, and nothing in the underlying numbers argues against it. The one thread worth watching is whether that 90.9 mph average exit velocity stays low as hitters accumulate data on a 100.4 mph fastball, because the swing-and-miss keeps the barrel rate down, and the profile holds as long as the whiff rate does.

reports.name: Jett Williams
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the thing worth watching here. Forty-seven walks in 358 AAA plate appearances translates to 10.8% at the MLB level, and that discipline is doing real work propping up a .341 OBP that a .234 average alone couldn't sustain. The power doesn't fully survive translation, a .151 ISO in AAA becoming .131 against MLB arms, so the profile hinges on whether the contact rate firms up enough to keep pitchers honest, because if the strikeouts hold at 23% while the raw power shrinks, there's not much margin left. Twenty-one stolen bases in the same sample give him a speed dimension that matters in a bench or platoon role, which is honestly the ceiling here: a useful piece against the right matchup, and a depth option if it isn't.

reports.name: Brandon Pfaadt
reports.published_report: The xERA sits at 3.82 and the contact profile is genuinely suppressed, with hard-hit rate at 36.5% and barrel rate at 8.2%, but none of that matters if he can't miss bats: a 15.6% strikeout rate and 20.1% whiff rate are deep in the bottom tier of the league, and the walk rate at 6.6% is the only reason those contact numbers even get to breathe. He's essentially a control-over-stuff pitcher with a 2475 rpm fastball spin that earns its keep against the swing plane, not against the swing. If the contact suppression holds, you get something close to a back-end innings-eater around that 3.82 xERA; if the league adjusts to the fastball shape without Pfaadt adding a strikeout weapon, the projection's 3.99 ERA over 133.1 innings is probably the ceiling, not the floor.

reports.name: Justin Wrobleski
reports.published_report:
The 3.57 ERA projection sits well ahead of a 4.51 xERA, and that gap is the whole argument about Wrobleski.

His walk rate is elite, 5.1% puts him at the 95th percentile, and that's genuinely load-bearing because a pitcher who doesn't beat himself buys himself margin for everything else. The problem is everything else: a 19.3% strikeout rate in the 28th percentile, a 19.6% whiff rate near the bottom of the league, and a 43.3% hard-hit rate that says hitters are finding the barrel when they do connect. The 2447 rpm fastball spin is a real asset, but spin without swing-and-miss is spin that's being managed, not dominated with. This profile works if the 32.4% chase rate keeps climbing and he converts more of that zone discipline into misses; if it doesn't, the ERA drifts toward the xERA and 154.5 innings of back-end starter production is what you're buying.

reports.name: Druw Jones

Five home runs with a .091 ISO translates to .097 at the MLB level, while the MLB average sits at .150, a gap that turns a passable line into a liability once the BABIP normalizes. Hitters who do make contact against him aren't doing anything with it, a 31.4% hard-hit rate notwithstanding, because 99.0 mph off the hand combined with that contact suppression leaves barrels essentially nowhere to hide. The K% at 26.0% and BB% at 8.3% are both right around league average for high-leverage work, so the whole profile leans on keeping the ball soft rather than blowing through lineups, and if that contact-suppression skill regresses even modestly, the strikeout rate isn't a safety net. He's a genuine high-leverage piece for Milwaukee, not a closer-in-waiting, but a reliever whose underlying quality is as real as a 2.45 ERA projection can reasonably promise.

The 18 home runs and .232 ISO at AA belong to a hitter who can do damage when he connects, but the ceiling stalls at a bench or platoon bat because the hit tool (.254 average, 58th percentile among this pool) almost certainly doesn't carry to an everyday role. reports.name: Keider Montero
reports.published_report: A 5.4% walk rate sitting at the 93rd percentile is doing a lot of carrying here, because almost nothing else on the Statcast card suggests a mid-rotation starter. The 18.9% whiff rate and 27.5% chase rate are both bottom-quarter marks, which means Montero isn't missing bats so much as he's refusing to give walks and letting contact management do the work, a recipe that produces a 3.51 xERA when it holds and gets exposed badly when sequencing turns against him. The projection buys it, 163.2 innings, 3.55 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, but 11 quality starts in a full rotation load is a thin cushion. Everything hinges on whether that command holds at a near-elite level, because if the walk rate creeps toward average he's a fifth starter on a short leash rather than a legitimate mid-rotation piece.

reports.name: Bryan Reynolds
reports.published_report: The tension in Reynolds's profile is right there in the Statcast card: a 13.8% walk rate sitting at the 93rd percentile, paired with a 29.0% whiff rate that grades out at the 25th. He earns his way on base at an elite clip, then gives a chunk of that contact skill back when he swings. The result is a .351 xwOBA that the 90.9 mph average exit velo and 46.7% hard-hit rate both support, while the .247 xBA quietly explains why the batting average never quite matches the underlying quality of contact. If the strikeout rate drifts higher, the whole profile leans on that walk rate to carry the OBP, and a .366 OBP projection off a shrinking contact base is a narrower margin than it looks. A true middle-of-the-order piece in a deeper lineup; in Pittsburgh, he's the lineup.

reports.name: Konnor Griffin
reports.published_report: The speed is undeniable and the contact picture is the question. Griffin's 29.9 ft/s sprint speed sits at the 99th percentile, and ValuCast's projection banks on that legs-first profile producing 24 stolen bases across a 327-PA season, enough to carry a .272/.330/.402 line into useful territory. The contact and discipline metrics tell a harder story: a 38.8% chase rate, a 31.7% whiff rate, and an xBA of .240 suggest a hitter who is getting to balls he probably shouldn't swing at and not doing much with them when he does. If he can bring the strikeout rate down from 26.3% and make the contact quality catch up to the barrel rate, the speed turns him into an everyday shortstop; if it doesn't, he's a bench piece whose legs keep him relevant but whose bat keeps him from mattering.

At AA this season, Jefferson Rojas is striking out just 16% of the time across 401 plate appearances, and that contact control translates to a 19.6% K% at the MLB level, well below what most big-league hitters run. The .266/.336/.453 slash with 15 home runs and 17 stolen bases fills out a profile that looks like a lot more than it's supposed to be at 21, and the .187 ISO at AA, even after it sheds down to .145 in translation, is backed by real contact rather than a .284 BABIP carrying the whole thing. The ceiling here is a bench or platoon bat, which sounds limiting until you note he's already showing average zone control at 21 with an 8.1% translated walk rate sitting right where the MLB average sits. If anything has to hold for the ceiling to reach its outer edge, it's the power translation, not the contact.

reports.name: Zebby Matthews
reports.published_report: The barrel rate is the story: 12.4% ranks at the 4th percentile, meaning hitters are making plenty of contact but almost none of it is doing real damage. That's a legitimately unusual profile, and it's the main reason a 20.2% strikeout rate and a 22.6% whiff rate don't sink him entirely. The 95.2 mph fastball gives him enough to work with, but the chase rate sits at 28.2% and the xERA lands at 4.64, so the ceiling here is a back-end starter who eats innings rather than misses bats. If that barrel suppression regresses toward league norms, the strikeout rate is too thin to compensate, and this becomes a swingman profile at best.

reports.name: Braylon Doughty
reports.published_report: The walk rate is doing something unusual for a 20-year-old at Double-A. Across AA & A+, Doughty has issued just 17 walks in 82.4 innings, a 1.9 BB/9 that translates to 2.6 at the MLB level while most pitchers are surrendering 3.2, and the strikeouts are sufficient, 100 across AA & A+, without being the headline. The 24% K-BB% is the number that earns the trust, because control this clean at his age typically survives a level jump even when stuff doesn't sharpen. The ceiling here is a multi-inning or setup reliever, maybe one to two years out, and the floor is depth; the whole read pivots on whether the strike-throwing holds when hitters at Triple-A start sitting on his secondary stuff.

reports.name: Adrian Morejon
reports.published_report: A 1.9% barrel rate against him, the lowest tier in the sport, is what the Statcast profile is actually about, and the 37.8% chase rate is what makes it structural. Hitters are expanding the zone and getting punished for it: a 34.5% whiff rate combined with 86.4 mph average exit velocity means the contact that does happen is soft. The 2.46 xERA is the honest read on what he's been worth, and 94 strikeouts across 80.4 projected innings with a 6.0% walk rate at a 2.97 ERA suggests the Padres have a late-inning weapon who profiles closer-adjacent even without the closing role.

reports.name: Xavier Isaac
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the whole argument. At AA in 359 plate appearances, Xavier Isaac has drawn 68 walks against 103 strikeouts, a 19% clip that translates to 13.7% at the MLB level — roughly 60% above what the average big leaguer posts at 8.5%. The .248 ISO at AA becomes .175 in translation, enough thump for a first baseman if not a carrying tool. The catch is a 29% strikeout rate that also travels intact at 29.1% MLB-equivalent, and at first base there's no defensive cushion absorbing contact trouble, so the whole profile hinges on the plate discipline holding and the power showing up together. If both land, he's a low-end everyday first baseman; if the strikeouts win, the walks keep him around as a high-OBP bench piece, nothing more.

reports.name: Connor Prielipp
reports.published_report: The fastball sits 95.5 mph and grades into the upper tier of the league, but hitters are squaring him up at 90.4 mph average exit velocity, one of the lower contact-quality marks you'll see from a pitcher in a rotation. The 4.04 xERA says he's roughly league-average in aggregate, and the projection's 4.47 ERA over 118.3 innings reflects a back-of-the-rotation arm who isn't making hitters uncomfortable enough. reports.name: Justin Gonzales
reports.published_report: The discipline is the loudest thing in this profile. A 19-year-old posting a 14 BB% and 19 K% at A+ is controlling the zone at a level most teenagers in full-season ball never approach, and the .390 OBP across 387 plate appearances isn't riding a hot BABIP at .299. The translation muddies it, though: that walk rate becomes 10.3% in MLB terms, which holds up fine, but the ISO shrinks from .188 at A+ to a translated .135, meaningfully short of what MLB corner hitters need to profile as regulars. If the power answer is "it isn't there," what remains is a patient right-field bat with fringe-regular offensive production, a bench piece who gets on base rather than an everyday corner.

reports.name: Logan Henderson
reports.published_report: A 2.60 xERA with a 5.2% walk rate is a genuine ace profile, and Henderson is producing it without overpowering anyone. The fastball sits 93.0 mph, well below the current big-league standard, so a 32.3% K rate is doing something structurally unusual: he's missing bats at an elite clip without elite velocity, and the .252 xwOBA says the underlying contact quality matches the strikeout story. His chase rate of 29.8% is pedestrian, which means the strikeouts come from contact-avoidance inside the zone rather than from expanding it, a fragile foundation if hitters adjust and start squaring him up. The projection at 3.21 ERA over 91.5 innings reflects something like a midseason debut or usage caution, and if he sustains this Statcast level over a full workload, he's a number-two starter; if the zone-whiff approach gets exposed as hitters get more looks, you've got a very good reliever.

Torin is putting up an 11 K% across 416 PA at AA, and the MLB-equivalent translation puts his strikeout rate at 15.9%, which is how a hitter gets to a roster when most major-league hitters fan far more often. The power and patience don't follow: his .144 ISO at AA translates to .123 at the major-league level, and his 8 BB% at AA comes out short of where it needs to be in translation, leaving an OPS environment that doesn't play. If the contact translates and some gap power develops with age, he's a second-division regular who hits for average and runs a bit; if the bat-to-ball skill is the whole profile and the power never fills in, what's left is a bench piece whose ceiling is mostly about not striking out.

reports.name: Yandy Díaz
reports.published_report: The contact profile here is quietly elite, and the power has been a long time coming. A 14.4% whiff rate places him in rarefied company for a corner bat, and he pairs it with 47.7% hard contact, which explains why the xBA sits at .283 even without a sprint-speed-fueled infield-hit bonus. The projection's .824 OPS across 688 plate appearances reflects a hitter whose underlying metrics have always promised more pop than the counting stats delivered, and at 34, with 22 projected home runs, it looks like the translation has finally arrived. The one dependency worth naming: his barrel rate is just 7.0%, so the power rests almost entirely on sustaining that volume of hard contact rather than on peak thump, and any erosion in bat-to-ball quality would pull the slugging line down faster than the contact skills could compensate.

reports.name: Blake Mitchell
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the loudest thing in this profile, and it's also the thing that doesn't survive the translation. At A+ in 2026, Blake Mitchell is drawing 94 walks across 413 plate appearances, a 23% BB% that sits at the 99th percentile of his peer pool, paired with 20 home runs and a .426 OBP. But run those rates through an MLB equivalency and the walk rate cools to 15.4%, the strikeout rate climbs to 34.5%, and the ISO lands at .163, just above a league average that sits at .150. The whole profile hinges on whether a catcher who strikes out 32% of the time at A+ can trim that enough at higher levels to keep the on-base edge meaningful, because if the strikeout rate balloons rather than the walk rate holds, there's a bench bat left, and ValuCast's +3.1 score move in three days reads like the market pricing the ceiling before the hard part starts.

Across AA & A+, 61 walks in 373 plate appearances pushes the OBP to .391, and the ISO sits at .244, which translates to .163 at the MLB level — meaningful pop from a 20-year-old catcher. The concern is the strikeout rate: 92 strikeouts in the same sample translates to 27.5% in MLB context, well above the 22.0% MLB norm, meaning the hit tool has to stay functional for the power and patience to matter. If the contact doesn't firm up, you're left with a catcher who walks and sells out for power but can't put enough balls in play to force a lineup spot, which is the org depth floor the profile already names as a real possibility.

reports.name: Caden Bodine
reports.published_report: A 6% strikeout rate across 424 plate appearances at AA & A+ & A is the kind of contact profile that stops scouts mid-sentence. Caden Bodine has 24 strikeouts against 37 walks on the season, and the MLB-equivalent translation puts his K% at 11.8% while the typical big-leaguer sits at 22.0%. The power doesn't translate nearly as cleanly, his .16 ISO across AA & A+ & A becoming something closer to .119 in MLB context, below the 22.0% strikeout crowd's production baseline, so the entire profile hinges on whether the bat-to-ball skill is so extreme it compensates for modest raw power at a catching position where offense is scarce. If it does, there's a real everyday piece here despite a ceiling that currently reads bench or platoon bat; if the power gap proves too wide at the highest level, the contact rate becomes the best thing about a backup catcher.

reports.name: Santiago Suarez
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the whole profile. Eleven walks in 92 AA innings translates to a 1.9 BB/9 MLB-equivalent, and that control grades at the 99th percentile in his pitcher pool — a genuinely unusual skill at 21. The catch is that the strikeout stuff doesn't travel the same way: 77 punchouts across those same 92 innings look fine at this level, but the MLB translation lands at 7.0 K/9, and the resulting K-BB% of 12.9% sits right at what a replacement-level MLB arm produces. If the command holds and the stuff develops, he's a back-end starter; if the stuff stays where it is, the control alone makes a durable depth arm rather than a blank.

reports.name: Francisco Lindor
reports.published_report: The contact metrics and the counting stats are telling two different stories. Lindor's 91.6 mph average exit velocity and 48.6% hard-hit rate describe a hitter who still squares the ball with real authority, and the .448 xSLG backs that up, yet the projection lands at .241/.321/.432 — a line that's useful but no longer star-adjacent. The gap lives in his sprint speed, which at 26.6 ft/s has eroded enough that balls he used to beat out are outs now, and the .252 xBA reflects a hitter whose batted-ball quality isn't translating into average the way it once did. Eighteen projected home runs across 458 PA from a shortstop still carries lineup value, but this profile hinges on whether the hard contact keeps showing up at the same rate as the athleticism continues to fade.

reports.published_report: The walk rate is the one thing working here, and it's working hard. The problem is that the strikeouts don't back it up: 83 punchouts in those same 95.3 innings translate to a 7.2 MLB-equivalent K/9, and a K-BB% that comes out to 11.5% where the league runs 13.5%. If the command holds and the stuff finds a little more swing-and-miss, there's a back-end starter in this profile; if the strikeout rate stays where it is, what's left is a depth arm whose location keeps him from getting hit too hard but not from getting outmatched.

reports.name: Vinnie Pasquantino
reports.published_report: The contact-and-walk profile is legitimately useful, and everything else is a drag on it. A 16.2% whiff rate and 11.0% walk rate are both well above the middle of the league, and together they describe a hitter who controls the strike zone about as well as most regulars at the position. The problem is that the contact isn't doing enough damage — a 6.8% barrel rate and 39.7% hard-hit rate sitting in the low-40s percentile-wise means he makes contact on his terms but rarely punishes it, and the projection reflects that arithmetic honestly: .239/.322/.374 with 11 home runs across 480 plate appearances is a low-end regular's line, maybe a second-division starter with a generous home park. The whole profile hinges on whether the swing-and-miss suppression keeps him on the field while the power quietly ticks up, because if the discipline erodes or the gap between contact quality and contact rate doesn't narrow, what's left is a slow first baseman hitting for an OPS that has no business anchoring a lineup.

reports.name: Lucas Braun
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the one thing working in his favor, and it's genuinely working. Across AAA & AA in 2026, Lucas Braun has posted a 2.6 BB/9 over 94.4 innings, which translates to a 2.9 MLB-equivalent mark — a tick better than MLB average, and a real asset for a profile that needs every edge it can find. The problem is the other side: 82 strikeouts across 17 starts produce a 7.8 K/9 that translates to 7.3 at the MLB level, short of average, and the K-BB% of 14% here becomes 11.5% in translation. Everything hinges on whether the command advantage is enough to compensate when hitters don't miss, and at a ceiling of depth arm, what's left if it doesn't is a back-end roster option who survives on avoiding baserunners rather than retiring hitters cleanly.

The .295/.411/.543 line is backed by a .291 BABIP, so there's no luck tax coming due, and the .248 ISO across A+ & A translates to .154 at the MLB level, right at what the average big leaguer produces. If the plate discipline holds as competition stiffens, he becomes an everyday center fielder; if the contact rate quietly erodes against better secondaries, what's left is a bench bat who walks enough to stay on a roster but doesn't punish mistakes consistently enough to start.

reports.name: Marvin Alcantara
reports.published_report: The stolen bases are doing heavy lifting here. Fifteen at AA in 306 plate appearances is genuine production, but the rest of the offensive profile is thin enough that it can't carry the profile alone. His MLB-equivalent translation puts ISO at .119 where the average sits at .150, and his walk rate translates to 6.8% where the average sits at 8.5%, meaning the .238/.288/.368 AA line reflects a hitter who misses bats at a manageable rate but without the on-base skills or power to profile as more than a fringe regular. If the legs translate and the walk rate creeps up, he's a useful bench piece who gives a roster a specific skill; if neither develops, this is organizational depth at second base.

reports.name: Dalton Pence
reports.published_report: The 2.9 ERA across AAA & AA & A+ is doing a lot of heavy lifting for a profile that doesn't translate cleanly to a rotation spot. Dalton Pence has logged 81.3 innings with a 1.2 WHIP and 92 strikeouts against 30 walks, and the control picture is genuinely better than the raw walk total suggests — his BB/9 sits in the 79th percentile of the pitcher pool, and a 19% K-BB% reflects real competitive balance. The MLB-equivalent translation puts him at roughly 8.3 K/9 and 3.5 BB/9, both essentially at league average, which means the ERA won't follow him north if the margins don't tighten. If the command holds and the strikeout rate finds another gear, there's a back-end starter or high-leverage arm in there; if it doesn't, what's left is a depth arm.

reports.name: Jadher Areinamo
reports.published_report: The power profile at AA is the most interesting thing here, and also the thing that shrinks the most on translation. A .189 ISO across 293 PA at AA reads well on the card, but the MLB-equivalent drops to .146, roughly what a league-average bat produces, and the walk rate translates to 6.6% against a baseline that most big-league regulars clear comfortably. The contact side is quieter than the raw line suggests: a .277 BABIP holding up a .256 average, with 57 strikeouts kept manageable but an OBP of .302 that leaves almost no margin. If the power stays near that translated floor and the walk rate doesn't grow, what's left is a middle-infield profile that fits a bench role more than a lineup spot.
